about: Evidence-labelling cases for deep evaluation: given what a source says, which claim (type, status, value, variant_match) should the evaluator write? Labelling is where an AI evaluator is most likely to overstate evidence, so these cases target that. Grade a run by comparing the claim written to 'expected'. 'never' lists answers that are wrong.

cases.evidence: Marketplace listing photo shows a CE logo on the box of a smartphone sold in Germany.
The FCC equipment authorization database lists the phone's FCC ID with the matching model number.
Brand page: 'built from military-grade aluminium'. No alloy or temper is given.
Owner review: 'The left earbud stopped charging after two weeks.'
Reviews shown on the 256 GB listing, but the person is buying the 128 GB variant of the same model.
An independent review site measured 18 hours of battery life using its published test loop; the brand claims 30 hours.
A blog with affiliate links to the retailer says 'we tested it and it lasted 40 hours'.

expected.rule: An affiliated source can't support INDEPENDENTLY_TESTED. Record it as a performance claim from the affiliated source with a limitation, or leave it out; don't let it outweigh independent tests.

cases.evidence: Searched the spec sheet, manual and listing: seat foam density isn't stated anywhere.
never: omitting the claim entirely is acceptable but worse

cases.evidence: A UK shopper; the only listing found is on a US site at 129 USD.

expected.action: convert to GBP with a dated exchange rate and say so, add shipping and import charges if known, or ask the shopper

never: putting a USD listing in a GBP request unconverted

cases.evidence: Product page: 'Designed to last 10 years.' No test or warranty to back it.

expected.note: not a durability measurement; warranty.years is the scored fact

never: presenting 10 years as the product's lifespan

cases.evidence: Government recall database: the stroller model's recall is marked 'remedy available' but still open.
The shopper says: 'I measured my knee height: 46 cm sitting.'
never: an estimate from their overall height when they gave a measurement
